fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're standing at the top of a mountain on Mahe, and you spin slowly in a circle watching the ocean and islands. When you complete one full turn, you've rotated through all the angles around your position — that complete turn is always 360 degrees. Today we're learning why angles around a single point always add up to exactly 360 degrees, and how to use this to solve geometry problems.

fields.teacher_script: Look at any point. Around that point, you can draw multiple rays (straight lines starting from the point). The angles between these rays are called 'angles around a point'. No matter how many angles you create around a point, they must fit together perfectly to complete one full 360-degree rotation. Think of a pizza cut into slices: no matter how many slices you cut, the pieces all fit together to make one complete circle.

fields.teacher_script: Now there's a special case you need to know. When angles sit on a straight line (not around a full point), they only go half-way around — they sum to 180°. Angles on one side of a straight line must add to exactly 180°.

fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're a tour operator in Seychelles planning a day trip to Morne Seychellois National Park. Would you use the same map to navigate the park's walking trails as you would to show visitors where Seychelles sits in the Indian Ocean? Of course not! Different maps show different levels of detail. Today we're learning how to read a map's scale and understand why some maps are better for different tasks. This is the foundation of map skills that geographers use every day. As we explore this, think about which type of map you would choose to find a specific hiking trail in the park, and which you would use to plan a journey across the ocean.

fields.teacher_script:
Every map has a scale—a ratio that tells you how map distances relate to real-world distances. On a map marked '1:50,000', one unit on the map equals 50,000 of those same units in reality. For example, 1 cm on the map equals 50,000 cm (or 500 m) on the ground. 

Here's the key idea: a large scale ratio like 1:5,000 means the map shows a small area with lots of detail—perfect for a hiking map of a single valley. A small scale ratio like 1:50,000,000 means the map covers a huge area but shows less detail—like a map of the whole world. 

Now think about this: when would you choose a detailed map over a map that shows a wider area? What kind of map would help you find a specific street in your town?

images.caption: A smaller scale ratio (1:25,000) lets you show more detail; a larger scale ratio (1:5,000,000) shows less detail but covers more area.

images.description: Side-by-side scale bar illustration. Left side shows a scale bar for a 1:25,000 map where 1 cm = 250 m, with markings at 0, 250 m, and 500 m. Right side shows a scale bar for a 1:5,000,000 map where 1 cm = 50 km, with markings at 0, 50 km, and 100 km. Annotate left as 'Small denominator = larger real-world distance per cm' and right as 'Large denominator = smaller real-world distance per cm'. Use consistent fonts and clear labels.
